prize_parts.citation: For the invention of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis, using reversibly terminated fluorescent nucleotides on clustered single molecules

statement.case_for: I have moved from B051 to B011. Sequencing by synthesis is a chemical invention in the strict sense: a nucleotide with a reversible 3'-blocking group and a cleavable fluorophore, so that one base is added and read per cycle, on single molecules immobilised and amplified in clusters. The mechanism is defined at the level of the molecule, it has been independently confirmed for fifteen or more years, and it created a capability the whole of biology now uses. Balasubramanian and Klenerman conceived and developed the Solexa chemistry, so a two-name credit is clean and leaves headroom under the three-person cap. Five members (Aqvist, Linke, Brzezinski, Zou, Sparr) already describe it as the cleanest attribution among the high-impact candidates, and it is the only configuration that two members of opposite scientific backgrounds, a computational chemist and the chair, prefer outright. In a field of eight dispersed first choices I judge it the most defensible place to converge, and it is the candidate where I must apply my usual standard (was the chemistry actually shown to work, and is the evidence unambiguous) and it passes.
statement.case_against: Sequencing is mostly a platform and medicine achievement, and some members will read it as physiology or medicine. A citation that rewards the reversible-terminator chemistry has to be written with care so that it does not read as a prize for the field or for the instrument. Attribution is contestable: Rothberg's 454 pyrosequencing was the first commercial massively parallel system, and Mayer and Ju contributed clustering and terminator chemistry, so excluding them will be challenged. The prize also depends on priority claims that none of us can settle from recollection and that the expert reports must settle.

responses.point: Aqvist lists B011 alone, credited to Balasubramanian and Klenerman for reversible terminators on clustered single molecules, with B005 and B012 as alternatives, and notes that Rothberg or Mayer and Ju may need to be revisited.
responses.response: I now agree with your first part, and this is the main reason I moved. Your wording, reversible terminators with cleavable fluorophores on clustered single molecules, is the wording I would defend, because it ties the credit to the chemistry and not to the platform. On Rothberg I think the narrow citation is the right answer: 454 pyrosequencing used a different, non-terminator chemistry, and putting it in the same citation would turn a chemical invention into a field prize. Mayer and Ju are the harder case, and I would want the expert report on clustering and terminator priority before excluding them. On perovskites, we both rank B005 behind sequencing for stability and attribution reasons, and I keep that view; it is not in my final configuration.

responses.point: Linke pairs B011 with B001, nanopore sensing credited to Bayley alone, as two ways of reading the genome, with B034 and B012 as alternatives.
responses.response: I agree with the Cambridge part and disagree with the nanopore part. The principle is real and mature, but a one-name credit to Bayley leaves out Deamer, Akeson, Kasianowicz and Branton, who are deceased in the case of Branton, and I cannot defend that boundary on structural or experimental evidence. Even if it were settled, the pairing would spend the cap on one theme and make the prize look like a field prize about DNA readout. I would answer the chair's question by saying that if no living, defensible set can be named for B001, it should come out of the configuration; I will not add it to mine.

responses.point: Chabes ranks B034 first, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, and treats the cereblon and molecular-glue arm as the strongest evidence of maturity, listing B011 only as an alternative while asking how much of it is chemistry.
responses.response: I take your chemistry-versus-platform question seriously and it is why my citation names the nucleotide chemistry. I also accept your point that the glue arm has the longest patient record, and that is a real step beyond what I said in round 1, where I treated the clinical verdict as early. My remaining concern is the one you raise yourself: a prize that spans PROTACs and cereblon glues reads as two discoveries, and Ciulli, Sakamoto, Kim, Gray and Ito stay outside under any three-name cap. The chemistry in B011 is no less defined than the ternary-complex chemistry, and its attribution is cleaner, so I rank it above B034 and would keep B034 as the next candidate if B011 stalls.

responses.point: Somfai pairs Buchwald and Hartwig (B053) with Liu (B012), citing 25 years of confirmation and industrial use, and doubts that base editing is new chemistry because a natural deaminase is repurposed by protein engineering.
responses.response: I agree with your doubt about B012 as a chemistry prize, and I share your concern about the 2020 CRISPR prize. On B053, I said in round 1 that it is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and I stand by that, which is why it is my first alternative. The question is Kosugi's tin-amide coupling and the overlap with the 2010 cross-coupling prize, which I cannot settle from the files. If the expert report separates Kosugi's stoichiometric precedent from the ligand-controlled catalytic amination of Buchwald and Hartwig, B053 is as defensible as B011. I would not combine it with B012, since the three-name cap is then spent on two unrelated parts, each with an open question.

responses.point: Brzezinski keeps B028 first, with Gray and Winkler, as a quantitative physical mechanism confirmed for over three decades, and lists B042 as an alternative with Schlichting as the third name.
responses.response: I accept your point that B028 is mature and rests on solid evidence, and in round 1 I did not oppose it on evidence. My question about breadth stands, because Dutton, Moser, Beratan and Onuchic, whom you name yourself, make the credit look like a line of work and not a single discovery. On B042, I agree that the chemical weight depends on time-resolved results that are still maturing. I therefore keep it only as an alternative, and the choice between Hajdu and Schlichting as the third name should be decided by the expert report on whether the concept or the experimental realisation was decisive.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts sequencing by synthesis as a chemistry prize rather than a physiology or medicine prize, and whether the citation can reward the reversible-terminator chemistry and not the platform.
Whether Mayer and Ju, or Rothberg, have a priority claim that the expert reports will show to be decisive, which would force a restructuring of the two-name credit.
Whether a single-part prize with two names can reach five votes when the eight first-round positions were so dispersed, and which second part, if any, would help and not dilute it.
Whether B053 is cleaner than B011 once Kosugi's precedent is weighed.
statement.conflict_note: Updated: my research on electron crystallography of zeolites and porous materials is close to B051, which I preferred in round 1. I have withdrawn B051 from my configuration, partly because of the 2025 MOF prize and partly because of this proximity, and I would recuse myself from any vote on B051 if the committee wished. I also remain a Stockholm University colleague of Peter Brzezinski, who has said he sees no conflict. I have no tie to Balasubramanian, Klenerman, Buchwald, Hartwig or the B042 candidates that is apparent from my profile. B042 is a method close to my own field of diffraction, so I treat it only as an alternative.
